text.p: Loctite Corp set up an auction process on Wednesday to sell itself to the highest bidder, but it's not likely that the company will find an alternative to the previously announced $1.2 billion bid from Henkel KGaA.
Sources close to the situation said they knew of no potential rivals to Henkel, a major Loctite shareholder, but could not rule out the emergence of new bidders for the Hartford, Conn., company.
Even if new bidders do emerge, Loctite's tight deadline for presenting new bids could be difficult to meet.

Loctite has set December 4 as the deadline for presenting new bids. Sources said it would be very difficult for a would-be buyer to complete due diligence and formalize a bid in what amounts to four business days in the United States.
Most U.S. corporations are closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and many will remain closed through the weekend.

"It is very clear that (Loctite) management is very receptive to doing a deal with Henkel. But equally (Loctite's) special committee is undertaking the traditional role of a special committee, which is to find the best price," one of the sources said.
"Why, if they had something going with someone else, would they have to jam a bid in over a long holiday weekend?," he asked.
A spokesman for Loctite declined to comment. "We are in a bidding process here," he said.

So far, about 10 top U.S. and European companies have been mentioned as potential Henkel rivals, but sources said those companies have avoided or outright refused to take the role of white knight because of Henkel's major Loctite ownership and board presence.
Among the companies, DuPont Co, Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co and Ashland Inc were said to have been approached by Loctite.
Officials of those companies have declined to comment.

Three weeks ago, German-based Henkel raised its bid for the 65 percent of Loctite that it does not own to $57.75 per share from $56, and turned its takeover proposal into a hostile tender offer. Loctite rejected the offer as insufficient.
Currently, three Henkel appointees sit on the Loctite 12-member board.

An arbitrageur said, "I don't know whether they have anything or not, but it (the auction) certainly is a tactic to possibly evoke a higher bid from Henkel." Analysts have said $59 to $61 per share would be a fair price.
And the possibility of an agreed merger seemed more likely Wednesday when Henkel said Loctite had agreed to open its books to Henkel.
Sources would only say Henkel is evaluating the new data.

"Henkel has three people on the board, who in the course of their serving the company are privy to information that they may or may not be in the position to share with Henkel management. As for information that was retrieved pursuant to the recent discussions, some of that was not available prior to that process," another source said.
"Put yourself in Loctite's shoes. Assuming they have nothing, what do they have to move Henkel higher except to bluff?," he said.
